identification.title: God of Wonders
identification.album: Offerings II: All I Have to Give
identification.notes: Written by Marc Byrd (Common Children) and Steve Hindalong (The Choir). Wikipedia says Byrd wrote the initial material in 1999 on a solo retreat in Arkansas and that Hindalong, wanting cosmic-scale imagery, shaped the rest from Book of Common Prayer language. First recorded on the 2000 compilation City on a Hill: Songs of Worship and Praise by members of Caedmon's Call, Third Day and Sixpence None the Richer. Third Day's live version, with extended tags, is on Offerings II (2002); it has also been recorded by Caedmon's Call, Rebecca St. James, Passion, Steve Green, Kutless and Shane & Shane, nearly 100 recordings by Hindalong's estimate. Publishers named by search listings: New Spring / Never Say Never Songs (Brentwood-Benson), Storm Boy Music, and Meaux Mercy (Capitol CMG); CCLI 3118757 per Lifeway and Hymnary listings seen in search results, not fetched. The list's guess of Third Day is right for the recording many churches know, but the song is the Byrd and Hindalong co-write and the release year is 2000 for the song, 2002 for this recording. Reviewed as the song, with note taken of the extended tags.

claims.structuralNotes: Two verses, a chorus that returns three times, and in the Third Day version an extended tag repeating praise of the Lord of heaven and earth with hallelujahs, then a closing tag. The first verse addresses God as Lord and creator of earth, sea and sky, with the heavens as his dwelling place, and gives him glory. The chorus declares him holy and beyond the cosmos, with creation declaring his majesty. The second verse is the singer's resolve to celebrate him in the morning and call on his name in the dark. The tag adds a request that the Lord reveal his heart to the singer and addresses Father and Lord God Almighty. The only act of God named is creation. Christ, the cross, the resurrection and the return are not reached, and the Spirit is not named.

strengths.title: Creation told as the ground of worship
strengths.explanation: The song grounds its praise in what God has made and in who he is, and does not treat wonder as a feeling. Creation is named as God's act, and it points beyond itself to the Maker.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The heavens declaring God's glory - the claim the verse and chorus build on.

strengths.title: The holiness and otherness of God
strengths.explanation: The chorus sets God as holy and above the cosmos he made, in the language of heaven's own worship. That keeps the Creator distinct from the creation.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Holy, holy, holy, with the earth full of his glory - the cry the chorus echoes.

strengths.title: Praise by day and by night
strengths.explanation: The second verse resolves to praise in the morning and to call on God's name in the dark, which gives the song room for the whole of a believer's life, hard hours included.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Declaring God's love in the morning and his faithfulness by night.

doctrinesAffirmed: God as creator of all things
The holiness and transcendence of God
The sovereignty of God over heaven and earth
Praise to the Father as Lord God Almighty
theological.assessment: Nothing to correct. The song is a creation hymn in contemporary dress, drawing on Psalm 19, Isaiah 6 and Revelation 4, with heaven as God's tabernacle a poetic image consistent with Scripture. What it does not reach is the gospel: Christ, the cross and the resurrection are absent, so it teaches who God is without saying how sinners come to him. No independent assessment of its content was found.

strengths.title: A simple structure a room learns quickly
strengths.explanation: Two verses and a returning chorus on a plain melodic line make the song easy to pick up, which helps explain its spread across nearly a hundred recordings.

strengths.title: A natural call to worship
strengths.explanation: Its subject is God's majesty in creation, so it suits an opening of a service or an occasion of wonder.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Published in several keys; Musicnotes lists leadsheets in G and F. Pick the key from the chorus for the room.

range.key: G and F (per Musicnotes listings in search results)
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The chorus returns three times and the extended tags repeat holy, hallelujah and the Lord of heaven and earth many times, so in the Third Day version repetition carries much of the closing.
communal.assessment: Congregational in words and form, and easy to learn. The tags can run long, and heavy repetition then does the work the words do not. A leader can shorten the tag to keep the song focused.

strengths.title: God is named as Lord, Father and Almighty
strengths.explanation: The addressee is never vague: the song names God as Lord, Father and Lord God Almighty.

clarity.assessment: Clear in its claims; its imagery is biblical and cosmic, and its meaning is not open to a wrong reading.

synthesis.summary: A creation hymn praising God as Lord and maker of earth, sea and sky, holy and above the cosmos, with a verse resolving to praise him morning and night and a tag asking him to reveal his heart. Its only named act is creation; Christ, the cross and the resurrection are not reached. Nothing in it is false. Heavy repetition in the extended tags is the delivery issue. No independent assessment was found.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The heavens declaring God's glory - the song's central image.
Holy, holy, holy, the earth full of his glory - the chorus's theme.
Holy, Lord God Almighty - the title the tag uses.
Praise in the morning and by night - the second verse's resolve.
